claim: Creative work cycles between generating rough candidate structures and exploring or testing them (Geneplore).
note: One framework (Finke, Ward, Smith book), seen only through snippets. Descriptive, no direct replication found. No LLM-agent application found (creative-b-22).

claim: When imagining novel things, people take a path of least resistance: they start from a known typical exemplar and keep its features.
note: Ward 1994 is the base study; Frith et al. 2022 only cites and uses it. Evidence for the human effect is old and rests on snippets. Agent rule: the first idea is the typical one.

claim: Showing examples makes people copy example features (design fixation), even when told to avoid them.
note: Jansson and Smith 1991, Smith et al. 1993, and a 2022 review agree. Caveat: examples that break basic assumptions can raise creativity (creative-c-13, essay level) and Sio et al. 2015 say conditions matter. Fixation is the default; it is not universal.

claim: LLMs fixate like humans: early outputs narrow later ideas; chain-of-thought reduced fixation in LLMs but not in humans.
note: Preprint, abstract only. Direct fit for a schema: fresh context per idea, not a growing list.

claim: Interactive brainstorming groups produce fewer ideas than the same people working alone; production blocking is the main cause.
note: Diehl and Stroebe 1987 (22 experiments reviewed), Mullen et al. 1991 meta-analysis, Stroebe et al. 2010 review. Evaluation apprehension hurt individuals but did not explain the group gap (creative-a-11). Mullen effect sizes not retrieved. Agent rule: generate in independent, isolated calls, then pool.

claim: The number of ideas generated is unrelated to the quality of the idea finally chosen, and people prefer feasible ideas over original ones when selecting.
note: From an abstract of a review. Challenges the common 'more ideas, then pick' assumption. Needs a second source.

claim: Incubation (setting a problem aside) has a small positive effect (about 0.29), larger for divergent tasks than for insight tasks, smaller when the break is filled with a demanding task.
note: All lines trace to Sio and Ormerod 2009 (one meta-analysis). Credible but not triangulated. For an LLM there is no clear analogue of a break, so transfer is speculative (a context reset or a later revisit).

claim: Creativity training and enhancement methods raise creativity scores, but the size is uncertain: 0.64 (older review), 0.53 (2023), and only 0.29 to 0.32 after correcting for publication bias (2024).
note: Direction is established; magnitude is contested downward. The 2024 meta-analysis is the most credible. Haase 2023 reports convergent-aimed methods beat divergent-aimed ones (k=11 only), which fits poorly with the incubation finding that divergent tasks gain more (creative-a-16 vs a-14). Do not trust the subtype split.

claim: Mednick's flat associative hierarchy predicts creativity; it was later questioned.
note: Snippet level, with only a pointer to the questioning. Treat as a weak hypothesis.

claim: Remote Associates Test measures convergent association and is a poor measure of LLM creativity (training contamination, limited validity).
note: Contamination claim comes from a search summary only; validity claim from low-credibility snippets.

claim: Across LLMs, answers to open-ended prompts are homogeneous: one model repeats itself, different models agree, and larger models are often less diverse.
note: Jiang et al. 2025 (benchmark), Zhang et al. 2025 (20 models), Deng et al. 2026 (preprint), Verdoorn 2026 (preprint). Matches our NoveltyBench result. Agent rule: forced divergence is needed on open tasks.

claim: Giving LLM ideas to humans raises rated novelty and usefulness of individual stories but makes the set of stories more similar.
note: All from Doshi and Hauser 2024 (RCT, 293 writers, fetched). Strong study, but one study. Low-creativity writers gained most. Consistent with the Hivemind findings, which supports the set-level part.

claim: Expert blind reviewers rate LLM research ideas as more novel than human ideas, but when executed the LLM ideas lose more score and rankings often flip.
note: Two stages of one research group (Si et al.). Strong designs (blind review, executed ideas) but one group. The execution gap is the key warning: novelty without feasibility checking.

claim: LLM judges and reward models are poorly calibrated on outputs where humans disagree, and LLM self-evaluation of ideas is weak.
note: Jiang et al. 2025 and Si et al. 2024 are independent. Agent rule: do not let the same model rank its own creative outputs as the only filter.

claim: Asking for a set of answers with stated probabilities (verbalized sampling) raises diversity in creative writing by 1.6 to 2.1 times, more for capable models; the authors blame typicality bias in preference data.
note: One preprint, three lines. Cheap and testable in our harness. Typicality-bias explanation is a hypothesis.

claim: Prompting for creativity or reasoning raises scores on a divergence task but leaves diversity across trials flat; widening the sampling pool raises diversity without a matching score gain.
note: One preprint (Verdoorn and Paperno), 5 models. Says quality-of-one-answer and diversity-across-answers are separate dials.

claim: Temperature is only weakly correlated with novelty and moderately with incoherence, so it is not a real creativity dial.
note: Peeperkorn et al. used one model and one task. Verdoorn found wider sampling pools did raise diversity for most models. The two do not strictly conflict (novelty vs cross-trial diversity), but the point is unsettled.

claim: Persona-conditioned generators restore diversity across LLM outputs.
note: Wan and Kalman (preprint, 10 personas) and a low-quality white paper support it. Deng et al. found ordinary personas gave more partitioned knowledge than creative-expert personas, so persona content matters. Diversity is judged by LLMs in some of these. All preprint or weaker.

claim: Thinking models and general intelligence do not reliably predict creativity or idea generation quality.
note: CREATE (not checked beyond abstract), LiveIdeaBench (LLM panel judges), Zhang 2025, Verdoorn 2026. Several are preprints; judges are LLMs. Supports: more thinking tokens is not a creativity strategy.

claim: LLMs beat the average human on the Divergent Association Task but stay below highly creative humans.
note: Large human sample, but the task is a narrow word-distance test.

claim: Far combinations or analogies reliably raise novelty but not reliably quality; near analogies can serve quality better, at least for designers without analogy training.
note: Chan and Schunn 2015 (lab plus field) and a 2019 study of 84 students (counted once; b-20 and c-16 are the same study). Both from snippets. Agent rule: far mixing then a feasibility filter, not far mixing alone.

claim: In multi-agent idea generation, interaction structure matters more than agent count; authority-led groups give less diversity and more agents give diminishing returns.
note: Preprint 2026, not checked beyond the page. Fits the human blocking and authority literature but is not independent confirmation.

claim: LLM help may hinder independent creative performance when people later work without the tool.
note: Two pre-registered experiments (1,100 participants). Relevant to human-in-loop, only weakly to a standalone agent.

claim: Agent pipelines built on combinatorial-creativity theory (cross-domain retrieval) improve similarity to real research developments; 35-LLM benchmark says models are better at analogies than at concept blends.
note: Snippet-level, one line has unconfirmed authors (credibility 30). Do not use for design without opening the papers.

claim: Verbalizing a solution while working can impair insight problem solving (verbal overshadowing).
note: Memory only, not verified. Known to have replication concerns in the wider verbal overshadowing literature; treat as unverified.
